This was the second visit Mr. Ronning has undertaken to Hanoi on the initiative and
Inquiries of the Ministry instructions of the Canadian government. His first visit, as the house will recall, took place last March.

I can say, however, that Mr. Ronning's assignment was conceived with two related objectives in mind; first, to see whether a basis could be established on which the parties primarily concerned in the Viet Nam conflict might be enabled to enter into direct informal discussions; and second, to continue to explore the attitudes of interested governments on the various elements which might in due course constitute the basis for a peaceful solution of the Viet Nam situation.

I rise to speak on the first vote of the labour estimates because I respectfully suggest that there are matters in the labour field in Canada which need emphasis. In addition, there are matters respecting labour legislation in Canada which need to be stated here and certain actions and courses taken by employers need emphasis also at this time. I want to refer first of all to something members of this party have said on a number of occasions, that the basic reasons for labour unrest in Canada today appear in the main to be two. The first is the rise in the cost of
[The Chairman.]
living in the last couple of years and the second is the feeling of fear that workers in Canada have about the security of their jobs resulting from the technological changes known as automation.
I think it is unfair to blame unions and workers for insisting on improvements in their standard of living and for insisting on improvements in their wages and fringe benefits in view of this situation. It is usual for many people in Canada to blame labour in major part, if not in total, for the increases in prices. It is my submission that every study which has been made of the role of wages in the cost of living has shown that increased wages are not responsible for the increased prices in this country. In addition, every study which has been made has emphasized that it is inaccurate to suggest that the rise in wages in Canada has been responsible for making Canada uncompetitive in foreign markets, and that the contrary is true.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, without taking a great deal of time, let me point out that every study made by the Economic Council and by the research men in the minister's department indicates that there has been a very huge increase in productivity per man hours of labour in Canada since the end of the second world war. These studies show, for example, that from the 1935-39 period immediately before the second world war to 1963 there was an increase in the labour cost per unit output in manufacturing of 135.4 per cent. When that is adjusted to take into account the reduction in exchange rates it comes down to about 118.3 per cent.
From 1946 to 1953 the increase in cost per unit went up only by 50 per cent. On the other hand, from 1960 to 1963 the percentage trend was downward and there was an actual reduction in labour costs per unit of 1.4 per cent. This reduction was around 11.3 per cent if one makes the adjustment because of the change in the exchange rate. The fact is that labour costs per unit of output in Canada dropped very considerably between 1960 and 1963. The Economic Council, which made these calculations and found that the labour cost per unit of output in manufacturing decreased, as I have said, by 11.3 per cent from 1960 to 1963, drew this conclusion:
Canadian unit labour costs in manufacturing over recent years have also risen substantially less than in most other leading industrially advanced nations.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
After the Economic Council had pointed out the reduction in the Canadian exchange

rate and the effect which it had it went on to say in its report:
Another important factor has been the relatively much smaller average increases in wages in Canada than have recently been occurring in most European countries.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, the United States is the only country in which the increase in wages from 1957 to 1964 was about equal to that in Canada. If I remember correctly, I think that on the average the increase was 4.4 per cent annually in Canada and about 4.3 per cent in the United States. In the other countries included in the various studies to which I have referred we find that the increase in wages in the United Kingdom was an average of 5.9 per cent over the same period, in Sweden 8.8 per cent, in The Netherlands 10 per cent, in France 11.1 per cent, in Italy 11.9 per cent, in Germany 12 per cent and in Japan 17.2 per cent. Among these nations are, of course, most of our competitors in the international commodity market. In all cases the rate of increase in wages has been substantially more than that in Canada, in some instances three or four times the Canadian increase over the same period.
Similarly, Mr. Chairman, if you look at the increase in the per unit cost as calculated by the United States department of commerce, according to the statistics which they have published, there is an equally revealing state of affairs as far as the Canadian situation is concerned. The percentage increase in labour cost per unit of output in manufacturing from 1957 to 1964 in Canada was 3 per cent while it was 5 per cent in the United States, 42 per cent in France, 23 per cent in Germany, 11 per cent in Japan, 26 per cent in The Netherlands, 16 per cent in Sweden, 16 per cent in the United Kingdom and 17 per cent in Italy. There again the increase in the labour cost per unit of output in manufacturing in Canada was the lowest among these countries which I have cited. In many cases their increase was five and even ten times as high as the increase in unit labour cost in this country.
I would remind the members of the committee, and through the members of the committee I remind my fellow citizens of Canada, that the per unit cost of labour is what matters, not the size of the increase in wages. If it is possible to increase wages and at the same time to introduce efficiency which lowers the per unit cost or avoids an excessive increase, then, Mr. Chairman, you have
Supply-Labour
the happiest of situations. The working people benefit from the advances which are made. Their standard of living is improved and at the same time the economic position of Canada remains in the preferred position in which it was before the increase in the wage rate.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I suggest we should realize when we discuss labour matters in this country that the arguments against labour and against the unions to the effect that they are pricing Canada out of the markets of the world are sheer propaganda. It may be true in one or two industries; I cannot say I imagine there are exceptions to the general rule; there always are. But by and large, in Canada's manufacturing industries as a whole wages have not, if I remember correctly the way the Economic Council puts it, been the causative factor in the increase in prices in this country.
I suggest, as was suggested previously, that the real causes of price increases in Canada have been on the one hand the administered price policies of many corporations and on the other the very large, almost phenomenal increase in the rate of profits, both before and after taxes, particularly of the large industries.
I set that, Mr. Chairman, as the starting point for a discussion of labour matters in Canada, and I plead with the members of this committee and with the people of Canada not to divide the country by suggesting that labour is being unreasonable and is pushing prices up. This is no more fair or just than to say that when the farmers of Canada do get a little bit more occasionally they are responsible for the increase in the cost of food, one of the major causes of the increase in the cost of living. In fact the increase in the cost of food is mainly due to the food processors and food packing industry, not to the primary producers.
The workers in the plants and in the mines are the primary industrial producers in the country. Like the farmers, and together with the farmers, they are in our view the victims of the same squeeze between prices and costs, of the same administered price policies and of the same concentration of wealth and power.
Another point frequently pressed in this country, as well as in this house on occasion, is that the workers continue to have their right to strike and to interfere with the economy of the country, etc., ect. Let me say first without any apology that I consider the right of people to say that they will not work

June 22, 1966
Supply-Labour
lor certain wages or under certain working conditions to be a basic right in a democratic country. There may be some exceptions to this in, for example, defence industries or where security matters are involved. But when the time comes when we prevent by law the ordinary worker, whether he be white collar, blue collar, professional, mine worker or industrial worker, from exercising his right to refuse to work under certain conditions and at a certain wage, then we abandon the basic precepts of democracy.
I urge hon. members to recognize that when workers and members of unions exercise their right to strike they are exercising a right which the Supreme Court of Canada, in the case of Zambri v. Canadian Pacific Railway which was heard a few years ago and in which I was involved, has held is a right which is theirs at common law, a right which has been restated in the statute law of this country and in the various labour relations acts.
I would also remind the committee that it is unfair and a great mistake to forget that the right to strike has in fact been very substantially curbed under every jurisdiction in Canada except the province of Saskatchewan, though I understand that some amendments may have been or are about to be introduced in the legislature of that province. In every other jurisdiction in this country, once a collective agreement is signed, then for the duration of that collective agreement, whether it be one year, two years, three years or five years, the right to strike is taken away by law. In such cases employees are prohibited from striking during the life of the agreement. Union officers are prohibited from counselling strikes. Both employees who strike and unions and union officers who counsel or initiate strikes are subject to prosecution, whether under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act passed by this parliament or under the labour relations acts passed by the provincial legislatures.
The fact is that before order in council 1003, which was introduced in Canada during the war, all workers in Canada had the right to strike whenever they decided in their judgment to do so whereas under the present law they can strike only after certain procedures have been followed. They can strike lawfully only after a collective agreement has terminated, after certain conciliation and mediation procedures are completed and a certain period beyond has passed. We have in

fact taken from the workers of this country their right to strike during the major part of their working lives, namely, during the periods when collective agreements are in force. I am not saying that this is a bad thing I believe, and I am sure all members of my party believe, that this was a step which brought some order out of chaos in labour relations. It introduced into the labour relations field the concept that once a worker made a bargain with an employer through his union and the employer made a bargain with him, then for the duration of that bargain both of them should live together in peace. If there are differences between them they should settle them by the grievance procedure or by arbitration if they cannot settle them themselves. Thus there is a useful introduction, if I may call it that, of a civilized relationship and civilized behaviour into the matter. The right to strike during the effective period is taken away.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The relevance of this to my next point is that because the right to strike is taken away during the life of a collective agreement, because the workers cannot do what they would have done under the common law, namely, down tools and walk out, or pull the plug as it is called, grievances build up during the life of the agreement. If those grievances are not settled to the satisfaction of the workers, bitterness and resentment are built up. Therefore, when the workers get to the bargaining table to negotiate for a new agreement or to revise an old agreement, nine times out of ten the union committee makes representations not only about negotiations but also about a backlog of unsatisfied grievances and unresolved complaints. The union committee brings to the table a mountain of complaints having nothing to do with the major part of the negotiations. I say that anybody having anything to do with labour must keep in mind that at the negotiating table you are dealing not only with particular questions of wages, reduction of hours or job security but also, whether you like it or not, with a build-up of resentment and bitterness resulting either from failure to solve complaints during the life of the agreement or from other factors which have produced a great deal of discontent and dissatisfaction.
This was one of the major problems in the longshoremen's strike. I have never acted for the longshoremen in Montreal, Quebec or Trois-Rivieres but I have acted for them in Toronto and Hamilton. I know from personal
June 22, 1966

experience at the negotiating table that it takes a couple of days to get rid of the complaints and the bitterness before you get down to discussing the issues to be negotiated.
Related to that-and this brings me directly to the department and to the legislation which the department administers-is the terrible prolongation of negotiations. The longshoremen's strike which was settled about a week ago had to do with revising a collective agreement that expired, if my memory serves me right, on November 30, 1965, some six or seven months ago. Negotiations were started before that. This sort of thing is true for almost every major set of negotiations. Our machinery permits either the employer or the union to drag his or its feet for months. It has been my experience-I am not impartial and I am therefore making this statement out of my particular set of premises and prejudices-that it is the employer who drags his feet. As a matter of fact, my information is that in the longshoremen's strike, until the Minister of Labour got into the picture some week or two before the final settlement, the union had not had any monetary offer from the Shipping Federation despite having gone through six months of negotiations. The union had not had an offer it could look at and consider.
I would not be exaggerating if I said that I have known hundreds of such cases where the employer, on the theory that if he starts too early he will have to give too much, withholds his offer until the last minute. And what does that result in?
People often blame unions, if I may interject this, as if they were impersonal corporations. I know that there are shareholders in a corporation and that there are members of the board, but the fact is that a corporation is a much more monolithic organization than a union. In the corporation a few persons are able to make a decision and the negotiators are told to carry it through.

We considered the step very carefully, Mr. Chairman. We felt three things. We felt, first, that the economic situation had reached a point in Canada where some legislative step was likely to become necessary. Second, we felt if a step was likely to become necessary it was better if it were by legislation which did not involve compulsory arbitration but which in effect gave the workers the monetary increase which had already, we thought, been agreed to. The final agreement showed that we were right, because 80 cents over two years is exactly what was agreed to and what our bill proposed.
In our bill the remainder of the differences would be left to negotiations and to a commissioner of inquiry. Thus the collective bargaining system would not be interfered with, as my friend suggests.
Also-and I know every time one says something like this some hon. members shout with guilt feelings that they cannot control, "You are being pure" and all such nonsense, which does not phase me-we felt that precisely because of our close association with the labour movement in Canada a step suggesting legislation of this sort might serve a useful purpose in promoting negotiations, in stimulating them and, if you like, in bringing those negotiations further forward. We knew that hon. members in this house would ask exactly those questions the hon. member asked and would say that we were trying to interfere with collective bargaining. None the less we believed, right or wrong, that our bill on the floor of this house, or the suggestion of such a bill, would serve a useful and constructive purpose in stimulating the negotiations and in suggesting the kind of legislation that should be undertaken, if legislation should be necessary at all.
I can only say to the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, that we were delighted to see the result produced by collective bargaining. Let me point out that the good result was achieved only after practically the entire cabinet was involved and after the Prime

June 22, 1966

Minister became involved in the negotiations. If you set such a precedent, too often the Prime Minister and the entire cabinet will be involved in settling labour disputes which ought to be settled without the involvement of the entire cabinet.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The question asked by the hon. member made me digress. I shall come back to what I said. 1 bring to the attention of the minister what I think is one of the matters that careful consideration should be given to, namely, that the time limits for negotiation and conciliation should be tightened. Since we already have law on the statute books dealing with this aspect of things, let us make the law workable. You can make the law workable only if the law sets very tight limits on the length of time during which the parties can negotiate directly before going to conciliation and, if conciliation is undertaken, before a final settlement one way or the other. We must in the future avoid the kind of lengthy, drawn-out process of negotiation and conciliation which can result and does result only in further bitterness, further resentment and a build-up of impatience among the rank and file of the union membership which makes it almost impossible for the bargaining committee to arrive at any conclusion which would be acceptable to union members.
We ought to look on the conciliator as being more important than we have hitherto done. Every conciliator ought to be of the rank of a mediator. It is not enough to sit down with the parties and listen to them, but carry no weight with them and have no influence with them. We should get the kind of conciliator who has a standing of great importance in the field of industrial relations, a man who has a knowledge way beyond that of the average conciliator today. He must carry weight with the parties.
I am confident as a result of intimate knowledge that the Air Canada strike could not have been avoided had not an experienced member of the Labour Department carried on the final phase of the discussions. I cannot pay too high a compliment to the excellent job Bernard Wilson did. I am confident that had it not been for a man like Bernard Wilson there would have been no settlement.
I would suggest too that a conciliator nowadays ought not to come to the bargaining table with empty hands and, if some of

them will forgive my saying so, with empty heads as far as the facts of the situation are concerned. I cannot blame them. At the present time they are given no information. I think conciliators ought to have the benefit of a research organization behind them. When a conciliator goes to the bargaining table to help the parties adjust their differences he ought to have more information at his disposal than they have, not just as much, about working conditions in the industry, about the wages paid, about the wages paid in comparative fields, the place of the industry in relation to exports, and so on. All these matters relate to the settlement of wage and related disputes and ought to be within the knowledge of the conciliator. Otherwise, he listens to one story, which is usually exaggerated and distorted, then he listens to another, which is usually equally exaggerated and distorted, and is often completely at sea about what is really in dispute between the parties. I therefore make these few concrete suggestions.
I wish to turn now to the question of the longshoremen and the Labour Code and to say briefly that the minister failed to understand the questions asked by my leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and the question I myself asked yesterday. We are not concerned with the latest court action. If the court found that the men violated an injunction order and felt they should be punished for doing so, that is a separate matter. What I am concerned with is that the Labour Code does not define an employee in adequate terms and does not make it sufficiently clear that people such as longshoremen come under the Labour Code, that they can as a matter of right refuse to work on the eight regular holidays mentioned in this code, again, that they have a right not to work longer hours than those provided by the code and that they have a right to refuse to work if they do not get the vacation pay which the code provides.
If we enact a law setting out benefits which workers in certain industries should enjoy, we ought to write that law in such a way as to make it impossible for employers to interfere with the rights of the workers. It is the first injunction I am concerned about, the fact that an employer was able to go to court and obtain an injunction forcing these men to go back to work.
The act and the regulations Should be amended so that the workers may be able to

About ten days ago the house, and especially the government members applauded with good reason the end of the longshoremen strike in Montreal. Throughout the house as well as throughout the country, everyone breathed more easily upon hearing about the settlement of that strike which had gone on for 37 days and had penalized, not only the parties involved, but practically all classes of our society in all the spheres of activity in the country. That sigh of relief marked, we hoped, the end of a very unhappy experience which unfortunately had resulted in nothing but misery, as is the case with most of the much publicized strikes.
At that time, we noticed in the ranks of the official opposition as well as in those of the other opposition parties, an almost complete lack of criticism because of the relief felt by everyone. However, that silence should not have been interpreted for a single moment as the expression of our satisfaction about the way the negotiations had been carried out or as a sign that we approved the government's intervention, because on that score, at least in all the corners of the opposition, I have the impression that everyone had felt a terrible disappointment. Now that the crisis is over, we would like to take advantage of this debate on the estimates to make known some of the serious thoughts we kept to ourselves then.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)

Since we were not able to make much comment at the time of the settlement of the longshoremen's strike I believe the time has now arrived when we can express our legitimate disappointment at the way the strike was allowed to continue and at the government's participation in efforts to settle it. How could we be other than disappointed when one stops to think that practically

June 22, 1966
Supply-Labour
everybody in the country was adversely affected by the strike action?
During the days preceding the settlement, and even during the days preceding the strike itself, we posed several questions to the minister asking what action he intended to take to bring about a happy settlement before adverse effects would have to be endured. Unfortunately his answers always contained an expression of hope but did not outline the kind of action that was needed.
One of the main arguments that was used was that the government should not butt into private negotiations. A lot can be said for that proposition, but now we know that no settlement was reached until the government did butt in. That should not have been a last resort; it should have been the first resort.
Aside from the private features of the negotiations, where strike action is involved we must consider that it is a form of economic warfare in which A argues it out with B and, if agreement cannot be reached, he then takes a form of economic action in order to have himself judged right. This is the general atmosphere of any strike, but when the welfare of the people of Canada is involved the government has a very definite responsibility. We submit that the longshoremen's strike was a sad experience from beginning to end simply because the government took no action to avoid having the strike take place. Mr. Chairman, you can imagine how scandalized and disappointed we were at the enthusiasm which rocked the aisles on the government side of the chamber when settlement of the strike was announced. This was the second time in two years that we saw such a reaction from government supporters.
Anybody who knows anything about labour matters knows that the time to applaud is when a strike has been avoided. A strike is a state of war, and nobody can win anything out of a war whether it be in the economic Held or in some other field. There is no reason to boast of a settlement. The time for boasting is when a strike has been avoided.
The same situation applied in the postal strike roughly a year ago. In that case we had nothing to gloat about but the fact that after everybody had suffered the government finally decided to do its little bit. I return to the point that government assistance should be offered before strike action is taken. Speeches were made to that effect before the longshoremen's strike took place, but to no avail. I repeat that the government has a
fMr. Regimbal.]
responsibility to step in when the interests of the economy are involved.
Would the hon. member permit a question? Does he know just what the government did during the six weeks or so that preceded the settlement?
We tried persistently to find out but we could not get a definite word in reply.

I thought the hon. gentleman agreed that contentious matters should not be dealt with in this house during negotiations since it might disturb things. Does he not think that applies equally to the minister and to the government, even though he might have liked them to make a statement on the subject?

I do not get the sense of the question, Mr. Chairman, since the minister had so many statements to make after the strike was settled. Why were we denied information until everything had been settled? All the government said in all its answers was that it hoped for settlement.
I remember mentioning in one speech during discussion of the estimates, also, I think, that without interfering in the actual process of negotiations the prestige of the minister and of the Department of Labour should be introduced as a factor with the negotiating parties who should be talked to in this general sense: Look, you can squabble all you like and fight all you like, but speaking for the people I must advise you I cannot allow any economic action to go beyond that.
There are several things that could be done in such a situation. In fact I experienced one recently. I was not the victim but just a couple of weeks ago I was returning through Paris from Geneva when Air France employees declared a two-day strike against the company one week in advance of the actual strike action. It was announced in such a way that the public could take steps to protect themselves against the inconvenience of such economic warfare.
It seems to me that the minister should have acted much sooner in the longshoremen's dispute because once a strike is allowed to start we all know that the eventual settlement is going to be twice as hard and as bitter to achieve. The parties at that stage are commited, have taken their stands and usually do not budge quickly from their positions. The government should act before the fact rather than after the fact. It should act
June 22, 1966

rather than just express the hope that the problem will go away. That is what it did on this occasion, but the problem did not go away and every class of society was affected.
Further, once the strike did take place the government's action left a lot to be desired. The strike was permitted to last much too long, some 37 days during which farmers, labour, management, industry and all classes of society were made to suffer. I come from a small town of approximately 10,000 population which contains four industries and all four were adversely affected by the strike. If that situation is multiplied all across Canada we can readily see what kind of economic tragedy a strike like this could have been and actually was.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
In any event, when the government finally decided to act it is our feeling that all the wrong people became involved and that the action during the strike could have been directed better. I am referring particularly to the crash committees which were organized. Everybody questions the participation by or the fact that certain persons were involved. Everybody agrees the Minister of Industry should have been there-this is a normal thing-even though several question his actual knowledge in the field of industrial relations. However, this is a question of principle to which no one had any objection. Many persons have raised objection to the fact that the President of the Privy Council was involved, because everybody believes he knows little or nothing about the whole field of industrial relations. Everybody knows he has been on both sides of the table, the management side and the labour side. Anybody in industrial relations knows that a person who tries to play both sides usually ends up using both sides against the middle, and the middle in this case happens to be the Canadian people who deserve better.
Another was the ex-minister of labour. We have doubts about him because if he was such a good minister of labour we suspect he would still be minister of labour. Everybody is miffed and mesmerized by the fact that the one person who knows more about labour than anybody in the government was not called upon. I am referring to the Minster of Citizenship and Immigration who has a record of a whole life of experience in this field. I can understand that there could be personal implications, that there could be political implications and that there could be
Supply-Labour
strategic implications, but it seems to me when any matter takes on the importance that this had we should drop these considerations and make sure that we send the best man in the circumstances to do the job.
The settlement itself certainly was not something we can crow about, mainly because we have just come out of the wonderful budget speech in which the Minister of Finance suggested very modestly to labour to please take their little old time and not insist on too many increases so that we can have a chance to settle our economy. Three weeks after that we come up with the biggest settlement that ever has been accomplished in Canada-30 per cent in two years. It is an amazing thing that we should find a contradiction like this within a few weeks and among the same people. Despite the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, without a doubt this is going to set a pattern for weeks to come. We dread the inevitable effect this will have on what everybody wants to be affected favourably, the cost of living. It seems to me a pattern has been set which necessarily will be followed in the negotiations that have broken down right now so far as the railways are concerned. Unfortunately you cannot get out of it too easily.
We are very disappointed with the way the strike was handled. We were very disappointed that the strike was allowed to happen and that it was allowed to last so long. Without being too pessimistic we fear that without a doubt we have just made the first step on a long path of suffering. It is on this particular basis that we very sincerely and modestly object.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to occupy a few moments of the time of the house in the consideration of the estimates of the Department of Labour with regard to an item concerning shift differential rates of pay which never came to my attention until June 13. This information was given me while serving on the health and welfare committee.
I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Labour to a situation which I think cries aloud for immediate remedy. I know him to be a fair man and I sincerely believe he will take immediate action and not put it off until some time in the dim and distant future when collective bargaining may be instituted for employees of the government.
When the postmen went on strike in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and elsewhere in Canada I said in this House of Commons that I supported the postmen in going on strike

June 22, 1966
Supply-Labour
for the simple reason that the government was telling them it could not pay them more money while at the same time it is the government which establishes the rates on mail and by keeping the postage rates down low the government is able to turn around and tell its employees that it cannot pay them more money because the revenue is not large enough. At the time of the strike I said, and I repeat it now, that when the cabinet was in a position to raise the rates to a fair and reasonable level they certainly were not justified in telling the post office employees that they could not raise their rates of pay.
We now have a situation in the Department of Veterans Affairs and in the Department of National Health and Welfare which I maintain cries aloud for correction. I believe it is the duty of the Department of Labour to step in. On two occasions I publicly have congratulated the Minister of Veterans Affairs for his administration of that department. I based my congratulations and commendation in large measure on the fact that they were providing a shift differential rate of pay to the nursing staff of the Department of Veterans Affairs hospitals across the dominion. Although I have been in business for 40 years and have been accustomed to shift differentials for workers who are working evening shifts or night shifts as opposed to the day shift, I never thought for a moment that the shift differentials being paid in the Department of Veterans Affairs were such that they cry aloud for immediate correction.
It is some years since I first began to agitate in public for a shift differential and day premium rate of pay for nurses on the staffs of our hospitals in the Dominion of Canada. In my investigation some years ago I was very pleased to learn that in the province of Quebec and in the province of Saskatchewan the hospital services commissions were paying shift differentials to nurses on evening and night shifts compared with the rate of pay for day shifts. This is not the case in the other eight provinces of Canada. In the province of Quebec the director of nursing at Notre Dame Hospital in Montreal told me about six years ago that the differential in the rate of pay was 12 cents an hour on the night shift and 15 cents an hour on the evening shift compared with the day rate. This was a rather interesting statement because of the fact that there was a higher differential for the evening shift than for the night shift. Normally the night shift draws the highest differential. I cannot remember

the name of the order to which this director of nursing belongs, but she told me that the nurses maintained that the shift from four o'clock to midnight interfered with their social life much more than did the midnight to eight a.m. shift, and for that reason the evening shift received a 15 cent differential and the night shift a 12 cent differential.
The province of Saskatchewan has had an equally good shift differential on these two shifts. So when it was announced in 1963 that the Department of Veterans Affairs would be paying a shift differential effective April 1, 1964, I, as a person interested in the matter, took it for granted that the rates would be in conformity with standard practice this country over or this continent over. I congratulated the minister and investigated the matter no further.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
However, when I was attending the committee on health and welfare considering the estimates on June 13 I asked the officials of the department who were then appearing before the committee whether they were paying shift differentials to nurses in hospitals for Eskimos and Indians which come under their direct control, in the same manner as the Department of Veterans Affairs. I was advised that they were paying the rates established by Treasury Board.
I am very glad that one of the officials who appeared before us on June 13 later sent me a letter in which he said:
At today's meeting of the national health and welfare estimates committee you asked me about the shift differential regulations. I thought you might like to have a copy of this.
He enclosed photostatic copies of the Treasury Board shift differential minutes. I was astounded to learn that the shift differentials paid by the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of National Health and Welfare for nurses are 8 cents an hour on the evening shift and 12 cents an hour on the night shift. While I may have been astounded to learn of these absolutely ridiculously low rates of shift differentials I was dumbfounded by the discovery that the Dominion of Canada does not pay the shift differentials for the full shift. In the case of the evening shift from 4 p.m. to midnight they only pay the shift differential for six hours, and on the night shift from midnight to 8 a.m. they only pay the shift differential for six hours from midnight to 6 a.m. The Treasury Board maintains that they are day work hours from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. and that
June 22, 1966

anybody who is working what the Treasury Board calls day work hours is only going to be paid day rates of pay and the rate differential will only be applied to six hours on the evening shift and six hours on the night shift.
I will read into the record Treasury Board action in this regard as indicated by extracts from the minutes of a meeting of the honourable Treasury Board held at Ottawa on December 12, 1963. It is headed "T.B. 609965 Treasury Board". It states:
The Treasury Board, pursuant to section 7 of the Financial Administration Act, is pleased to make the attached regulations respecting shift differential allowances effective April 1, 1964.
It is signed, I believe, by Mr. D. M. Watters. Attached is a Xerox copy of the shift differential allowances. Number one states that these regulations may be cited as shift differential allowance regulations. I will not read them in their entirety, but I should like to read 2(b) and 2(c) which are as follows:
(b)	"evening work" means regularly scheduled work performed by a public servant between 6 p.m. and midnight;
(c)	"night work" means regularly scheduled work by a public servant between midnight and 6 a.m.;
Section 3 reads:
Subject to sections 4 and 7, every public servant shall, in addition to his salary, be paid an allowance of 8 cents per hour for evening work and 12 cents per hour for night work.
These regulations are taken from the official Treasury Board regulations. This is a Xerox copy from which I have read.
Having been astounded, as I already said, by the minuscule shift differentials of 8 cents an hour and 12 cents an hour, I telephoned a reliable source of information in Montreal only last week with regard to nurses' rates of pay in the province of Quebec. This informant of mine is a man who holds a very responsible position in the hospital field in that province and he advised me that they pay a shift differential of $1.85 from 4 p.m. to 12 p.m. and that this shift differential applies to the whole eight hour shift. This differential is at the rate of 23.1 cents per hour compared with the 12 cents per hour shift differential paid by the government from 12 p.m. to 8 a.m. The Quebec hospitals pay a shift differential of $1 on evening shift for the full eight hours. This is 12.5 cents an hour. They are paying 12.5 cents an hour compared with the federal government paying 8 cents an hour and they pay 23.1 cents an hour compared with the federal government paying 12 cents an hour. I ask you, how in the name of
Supply-Labour
heaven these ridiculous rates paid by the federal government can be justified?
We pay the province of Quebec $200 million a year in equalization payments in order to help this have-not province. If they accept $200 million per year and can pay a differential of $1.85 per shift, surely to heaven the federal government, which thinks it is in a position to give $200 million a year to Quebec in equalization payments, should be able to match at least the shift differentials paid by the province of Quebec to its nurses. The province of Quebec pays its nurses a shift differential per week of $9.25 on the night shift but the federal government is only able to pay its shift workers a shift differential of $3.60 per week on the night shift. The province of Quebec is able to pay a shift differential of $5 a week and the federal government under comparative circumstances can only pay $2.40 a week for the evening shift. I cannot see how the Canadian government can ask nurses to work six hours in the evening for an extra eight cents an hour, which is 48 cents, because generosity such as that may ruin the country.
The first item in the estimates of the department refers to the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, to the administration of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, to the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act, to the fair wages policy order and to the Female Employees Equal Pay Act. When we are discussing legislation such as those acts to which these estimates apply, it is only right and proper that I should refer to these ridiculous rates of pay which have been authorized by the Treasury Board, and demand that the Department of Labour take a hand in this matter. Does 8 cents an hour for six hours and 12 cents an hour for six hours measure up to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code? Do these rates measure up to the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act? Do they measure up to decent labour-employer relations?
In reading the opening statement of the Minister of Labour made to the house on May 27 when these estimates were first introduced, I note that he referred to the fact that his work falls largely into three sectors, two of which are labour management relations and labour standards and benefits. Later in his remarks he referred to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code and stated as reported at page 5634 of Hansard for May 27:
I can say this, that the code has already had a very important effect in eliminating pockets of substandard wages-

June 22, 1966
Supply-Labour
I should like to see this code take effect in respect of these substandard wage areas relating to the 8 cent and 12 cent shift differentials paid in the D.V.A. hospitals and hospitals under the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Then the minister makes this interesting comment, as reported on the same page:
I should like to refer also to an increased activity in the woman's bureau of the Department of Labour. This provides a continuing focus in our department on policies and programs relating to the standards and conditions of work of women. The bureau aims...to promote working conditions in every industry throughout Canada that are conducive to the well-being of the women, and efficient production. The role of this woman's bureau is becoming increasingly important as more women, both married and single, enter the labour force.
I trust that I will not be criticized by anyone on this side of the house if I ask the women's division of the Department of Labour to consider this 8 cent an hour shift differential for six hours out of eight and the 12 cent shift differential for six hours out of eight compared with the $1.85 or 23.1 cent per hour shift differential that is paid in the province of Quebec on the evening shift and the $1 for eight hours or 12.5 cent per hour shift differential also paid.
Surely we can bring the federal shift differentials up to the same level as those paid in a province which is willing to be branded as a have-not province and gladly accepts $200 million from the federal treasury. This would bring these rates up to those which that province has set for itself as pie in the sky.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I do not believe that the comments I have made today are a reflection on the Department of Labour or on the Minister of Labour. I doubt very much if he is aware of the fact that wages of this kind are being paid. I draw your attention to the interesting comment made by the official of the Department of National Health and Welfare who sent me these xerox copies from which I have quoted. He makes this statement, that the responsibility for recommending amendments would rest on the staff of the Treasury Board. This is mighty interesting. I wonder if I, as an elected member of parliament, might not have some responsibility in recommending that the rates of pay under the heading of "shift differentials" should be altered and should be altered right away? I will never rest satisfied until the nurses of the Dominion of Canada are not only getting a decent shift differential but are

being paid day premium rates of pay for work performed on national holidays.
We talk about the tremendous shortage of
nurses in our hospitals. It is the most critical shortage in any single vocation in Canada, Mr. Chairman. It is a continuing problem for all doctors and all hospitals. It will never be settled until the rates of pay are commensurate with the services that these women give, particularly on the night shifts and when they work on holidays while other people are away enjoying themselves. I sincerely draw the attention of the Minister of Labour to these figures which, so far as I am concerned, were only disclosed on June 13. The minister made his opening statement on May 27. I am relying on his fairness and good nature to take the matter in hand right away.
When we tell the civil servants that when they get collective bargaining everything will be wonderful, we should warn them that there are many employees who have collective bargaining for whom conditions are not exatly perfect. You cannot accomplish much under collective bargaining unless both sides sit at the bargaining table and bargain in good faith. You can give the post office employees collective bargaining, but if you are not willing to raise the rates on mail matter you will tell the postal employees that you cannot raise their rates because you have not got the money.
If you are going to sit down with the hospital workers and tell them that you will only pay 8 cents an hour for part of a shift, then you are not approaching the labour problem in a fair manner when other employers who pay a shift differential are paying it for a full shift. These people have to be paid on a reasonable basis and not on the basis of this miniscule figure of 8 cents an hour for six hours on one shift and 12 cents an hour for six hours on another shift. I leave the matter in the hands of the Minister of Labour, since I believe he is a fair man. I do not belive he will delay in rectifying this ridiculous situation which has been placed on the record of the government by Treasury Board order of December 12, 1963, which became effective April 1, 1964.

May I have permission to put a short question to the Minister of Labour? It is a question and not a statement of any kind. As a result of information that has come to me, I ask the minister if he can inform the committee whether the R.C.M.P. searches which are now going on about the
June 22, 1966

premises of the Seafarers' International Union are in fact related to alleged irregularities on the part of the present officers of the Seafarers' International Union? I think the minister will appreciate the importance of this matter which I am bringing to his attention. I put the question as a result of information which I left the house in order to receive and I certainly hope the minister can make a report on this situation.

Mr. Chairman, it had been my intention to try to deal with points raised by individual members at the conclusion of all their remarks. I must confess, however, that in view of certain publicity that has resulted from the events to which the hon. member has just referred, namely, the searches that were made earlier today by the R.C.M.P. and may still be going on, I thought such a question might have been put to the Solicitor General or the Minister of Justice earlier this afternoon. However, I do believe that the members of this committee and the public generally are perhaps entitled to some information at this time, in view of the wording of the question which has been put to me.
I wish the Solicitor General or the Minister of Justice were here to give the answer, but they are not so I will try to answer. I can only say that it is not the practice of the Department of Justice or the Solicitor General to supply information about active investigations. However, I can say, and I think I should say in view of the way the question was worded, that the searches that are being made today are not related to the present officers of the S.I.U. but are related to the activities of the past president, Mr. Hal Banks.

Mr. Chairman, is rising to speak on the estimates of the Department of Labour I want to make it clear at the outset that any remarks I make about labour do not arise out of frustration as a result of past employer-employee relationships between this member and the minister, but perhaps rather reflect the general frustration one feels about employer-employee relationships in Canada today and the inactivity of the government in trying to resolve them. In the few minutes we have left before private members' hour, I must say I am somewhat surprised that the minister has brought forth the estimates of his department at this stage. In many ways he reminds one of the saying about certain individuals who tread where angels fear to
Supply-Labour
walk, especially in view of certain strike settlements that have dominated the headlines and the Canadian economy for the last four weeks as well as the pending strikes and unsettled labour situation which will dominate the Canadian economy and the Department of Labour during the summer months and early autumn.
Perhaps the minister might deserve credit for his courage in bringing forward his estimates now if there were no other labour disputes on the scene. However, if the purpose in bringing forward the labour estimates now is to cloak the disputes of the future and choke debate on the pending labour problems, then I suggest the minister is to be criticized for attempting to get the labour estimates passed at this time. In view of the participation directly or indirectly, and in both cases about which I am talking it became direct in the last stages, of the federal government in negotiations which resulted in the approval of a 30 per cent increase over two years for the workers in two recent labour strikes, the federal government has been a party to a precedent for the settlement of labour problems in Canada for the next while. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this precedent is going to be in effect an economic albatross that will be hung around the neck of not only the Minister of Labour but the government as well.
This 30 per cent increase in dollars and cents alone will bring wages close to the minimum wage ceiling in certain provinces. On what basis was the 30 per cent arrived at? I had some experience on the west coast with school boards and when settling wage disputes one looked at all the relevant factors. You looked at the increase in the cost of living, the increases in wages, the increase in productivity and you arrived at a contract that took all these factors into consideration. When you approve a settlement which involves a 30 per cent increase in wages over two years, over a contract that was settled two years ago and was satisfactory at that time, then you have the height of irresponsibility.
Unemployment may have been the bane of the former Conservative government and certain members of the present government stood up day after day and criticized the Conservative government about it. I believe it is the duty now of the opposition to stand up and, on a more specific aspect of the labour problem, bring before the house and the people of Canada valid criticism of an area in which the government has become involved

June 22. 1966
Supply-Labour
and with which it is going to have to live. I am afraid that, like the ancient mariner, the albatross is going to choke the government when it attempts the settlement of other labour disputes.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
We had an exhibition here by the Minister of National Health and Welfare the day before the longshoremen's strike was settled. The strike was then in its 38th day and there were 143 ships tied up in Montreal harbour. The minister stood up in the house and gave a learned exposition of the philosophy of collective bargaining. No one could take exception to that just as no one could take exception to the hon. member for York South saying this afternoon that people had the right to strike. However, Mr. Chairman, an exposition on the philosophy of collective bargaining by a minister who was the former minister of labour in the 38th day of a strike which tied up the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec, is something like the minister standing up and expressing his approval of motherhood. We are all in favour of collective bargaining and we are all in favour of motherhood. However, even dear mother, if she stalled her car on a highway and backed up 143 cars behind her, would be liable to a reprimand or to some help from the authorities. Even mother, if she stalls her car at an intersection when the green light is on, would be either reprimanded or given a little push by the authorities.
The mere fact that these authorities would reprimand mother would be no sign that the institution of motherhood was being attacked. In so far as mother with the car is concerned, you might take one police officer and help move her down the road. Here, however, we had the fantastic situation of the government, with all the cabinet reorganization that is going on, allowing five ministers to participate in the negotiations, including the Prime Minister. Referring again to the analogy with mother, I say that one officer might move the car if he knew what he was doing rather than have the whole police force help to move that little car down the road. I wish the Minister of National Health and Welfare were here because I felt some provocation to stand up and question him on his statement but the rules of the house did not allow it. How can the Minister of National Health and Welfare say that the process of collective bargaining, which is fine in principle, is working after a strike of 39 days, after 143 
ships have been tied up and when the government finally intervenes to help?
We had midnight seances. We on this side of the house thought that seances were a thing of the past in government. Here we have four or five ministers, including the Prime Minister, having meetings and looking for guidance. Finally, as a result of one fact or another, they resolved the longshoremen's strike. After the dissertation by the Minister of National Health and Welfare there was tremendous applause. The hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes remarked on this applause. I must say it rather got me. It would have made my grade 6 teacher feel great. I wish she could come here some time. I think she would have a lesson to teach all of us. She taught school for 52 years in one school. This is a fact. She happened to teach the man who was the principal, she taught my father and she taught many people before she retired two years ago. She believed in the principles of reading, writing and arithmetic. She had many pithy sayings and many fables. I know hon. members would be interested in one of the fables. I refer to that fable about the empty vessel making the most noise. I believe this could be applied to the applause which greeted the minister's dissertation on the philosophy of collective bargaining.
The minister's dissertation on the philosophy of collective bargaining was certainly punctured by having all those vessels tied up and this strike prolonged. I suggest that somewhere along the line the good of this country must transcend the competing and conflicting interests of combinations or groups of economic units. I am very sorry the Minister of National Health and Welfare is not here, because he was a very good professor. I am afraid he forgets, as other members of the government forget, that they are not professors now. They do not have to preach economic philosophy. They do not have to talk around the rights or wrongs of collective bargaining. They do not have to read textbooks on the subject. They are in the position of power and in the position of government. They are not in the classrooms but in the seats of authority where they should act. And they should act, and not agonize, in order to settle strikes before they happen rather than surrender responsibility after they have occurred.
That is just what has happened with hon. gentlemen across the way, and I am afraid with the Minister of Labour, certainly in the case of the longshoremen's and the St.
June 22, 1966

Lawrence seaway strikes. In regard to the longshoremen's strike, the minister asked the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes if he knew what the government did for the longshoremen. I would ask the minister what the government did for the seaway workers. I think that their acquiescence in the settlement of the seaway strike was more than an indictment of the inactivity of the government.
The position of the longshoremen did involve some cross-currents at first. But in the seaway strike the government appointed a Senator renowned for his prescience and knowledge of international law, but who I suggest, with all respect to him, has not mediated a labour dispute for years. Perhaps the minister would tell the house when this Senator last mediated a labour dispute, let alone a dispute affecting anything so involved and important as the St. Lawrence seaway. I suggest that the St. Lawrence seaway strike involves and indicts the government even more.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure the hon. member would want me to comment on the fact that he has referred to the St. Lawrence seaway strike three times. That matter was a dispute; it was never a strike.

The minister is quite correct, Mr. Chairman; it was not a strike and I thank him for that correction. But my point about the pending strike on the St. Lawrence seaway and/or settlement negotiations is this. The minister asked the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes to list all the things he had done. We on this side had been asking day after day what the government was doing. It is now clear what happened. So far as the St. Lawrence seaway is concerned there was never any intention to negotiate. It was merely a case of filling in a blank cheque; and that is what happened.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Does the hon. member, as a representative of a party which is supposed to be of pro-labour as well as pro-management sentiment, disapprove of the package deal that the employees of the seaway obtained with regard to parity of wages with those working on the United States side? Is he saying in effect that he disagreed with that settlement?

I am saying this, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Finance suggested certain principles should be followed to restrain

So far as I can see this government is not showing leadership or responsibility to the Canadian people at large. maintopic: ATLANTIC PROVINCES-NEW ENGLAND STATES AND WEST INDIES-SUGGESTED PROMOTION
ATLANTIC PROVINCES-NEW ENGLAND STATES AND WEST INDIES-SUGGESTED PROMOTION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of taking an initiative in promoting increased trade between the Atlantic provinces and such traditional market areas as the New England states of the United States and those islands formerly comprising the British West Indies.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by expressing a word of thanks to the house, especially to my colleague, friend and cousin, the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), who on Monday saved my spot or position on the order paper. Perhaps my position otherwise is not of the kind that can be rescued but I appreciate the action of the house and especially that of my colleague.
The motion which I have presumed to bring to the attention of the house this year is similar to a motion which I have brought forward on previous occasions in preceding parliaments. My earlier version was couched [Mr. Nowlan.j
in the terminology once used by the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) when he sat on this side of the house, which called for considering the advisability of establishing free trade between Canada and a portion of what used to be known as the British West Indies.
Since I have not succeeded in having that motion adopted even with the minister on that side, I have changed the terminology and therefore the direction of the motion somewhat and I am now suggesting that consideration be given to freer trade between my area, the Atlantic region, and some of its traditional areas of trade and of close relations other than trade, and I mention the New England states and the West Indies islands.
There has been, as hon. members may have noticed, in recent months some interest, especially in the province of the minister of health and welfare, Nova Scotia, in the question of considering out-and-out free trade between the Atlantic provinces of Canada and the New England states. A resolution was passed in the Nova Scotia House of Assembly to have this matter considered. There has also been some discussion involving the governors of some of the states of New England. It is not surprising that this interest has been stimulated to a degree by what has taken place in other parts of the country, namely, the establishment of what one might describe as free trade on a commodity basis. It is argued that if free trade between southern Ontario and northern Michigan in the form of the automotive free trade agreement can be operative, then so might free trade on a broader regional basis, namely, between the Atlantic provinces and New England, be considered.
There are, of course, difficulties in this situation. There might be some difficulties so far as control of the commodities are concerned once they have been exchanged vis-avis domestic trade.
With regard to New England, we must surely all be convinced that the economy of the Atlantic region of Canada is lagging, that it is continuing to lag, and that the lag between our area and the rest of Canada is broadening rather than narrowing. So if any way can be devised whereby we can facilitate the shipment of our goods and stimulate the output of our industries, this way should certainly be considered.
June 22, 1966

When I last spoke on this subject I suggested that we had perhaps reached the stage where another full-fledged commission of inquiry into our economy was in order, something of the scope and comprehension of the White or Duncan commissions. If such an inquiry were launched this general question of the stimulation of our trade should certainly be one of the subjects to receive attention.
I am not going to deal any further with the question of trade with New England, Mr. Speaker. I should like to confine the rest of my remarks more particularly to the other area which is mentioned in the resolution, namely, the West Indies.
It is not surprising that this initiative should come from one from the maritimes. Perhaps it is appropriate that it should come from one who is a resident of an island. The ties of sentiment, and of more than sentiment, between the maritimes and the West Indies are old. They used to be very strong and there are many of us who wish that they were stronger now.
This resolution is based on two considerations. The first, and I say this quite unabashedly, is the desire for an improvement in the economy of the Atlantic provinces. The stimulation of our seaborne trade is a very obvious factor in any such improvement. I do not have to belabour the house with statistics relating to this aspect.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Second, it stems from my own conviction that we must quickly upgrade our interest in the West Indies for reasons other than selfish or economic motives. There is a growing and, to me, disturbing disillusionment among some of the leaders in the West Indies. There was a very interesting and I think useful gathering at Dalhousie University last month in which leaders of the West Indies and of the maritimes participated. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) delivered an address. This meeting was a hopeful sign.
But if one reads the reports of this gathering one finds that the leaders of the West Indies, although in Canada, were not reluctant to make statements such as: "Canada is dragging its feet in the field of external aid." Those leaders suggested that they were hoping for some greater initiative in the development of broadening trade between the two areas.
We all want to be hopeful about the larger gathering which is to take place in Ottawa on
Suggested Promotion of Trade July 6. Being very hopeful I trust that this session will have adjourned for the summer recess before then so that nothing will interfere with the success of the meeting. We want to see that gathering successful.

speechtext:
That gathering will be between the heads of the Caribbean commonwealth countries and our own head of government. They will sit down to look in broad perspective at the problems of the Caribbean area and at the possibilities and prospects for improving relations, trade and other things between Canada and this area.
I do not want to raise any bogies and point out the great dangers existing in West Indian communities, now approaching political independence, owing to many of them having economies that fall far short of being viable. Some communities have achieved political independence. Indeed, some of the leaders of these areas point out the dangers which might develop in such a volatile part of the world because of such great economic poverty, political uncertainty and, shall we say, a proximity to a very dangerous part of the world, namely, Mr. Castro's Cuba.
We are concerned with these things as we look out to the world because we are a state which justifiably prides itself on its diplomacy. We seek to make our contribution in the field of foreign policy. Sometimes we almost suggest that we know the French better than the British know them although the British have dealt with the French for centuries. We sometimes suggest that we understand all sorts of people better than does the United States, which comes in close and daily contact with them.
I suggest that if there is any part of the world in which for us there is a combination of unique opportunity and superior ability to do something, it is in the Caribbean area. I know of no part of the world in which a limited degree of Canadian economic aid could be so helpful as in this area. I know of no part of the world where the failure of the have nations, to use that expression, to participate to the full could be more dangerous and explosive.
All that this resolution attempts to do is to stimulate what I think is a latent Canadian friendship and Canadian interest in the West Indies and the current problems thereof. There is a reservoir of good will between our peoples. There is a maximum of opportunity.
June 22, 1966

Suggested Promotion of Trade However, our external aid is not nearly what it should be. I do not think we have explored the possibilities of stimulating trade between the Caribbean and our country. We have let the "Lady" boats go out of existence and we have not replaced them. It looks as though private industry is not able or not willing to replace them. We should consider perhaps if it is not sufficiently important for Canada to return to some form of subsidy whereby we can use the Atlantic to carry goods north and south between these two areas.
We have made one forward step in developing air contacts. There are other forward steps. But I do not think we shall ever fulfil our destiny with respect to the West Indies if we look at the West Indies only as somewhere to have some fun in the sun if you can afford it, where you can drink good rum if you like it or put molasses on your bread if you are sufficiently old-fashioned.
