maintopic: ATLANTIC PROVINCES-NEW ENGLAND STATES AND WEST INDIES-SUGGESTED PROMOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his notice of motion the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) suggests that trade be increased between the Atlantic provinces and our traditional markets in New England and the West Indies. I feel that I must agree in principle with the proposition and I wish to take this occasion to put forward an extremely interesting proposal now promoted by a Montreal businessman, Mr. Kenneth Patrick, who is a former maritimer. I believe that Mr. Patrick's proposal is dynamic, colourful and makes a lot of sense. I am not saying that the government should adopt it in toto or immediately but I am saying that the proposition deserves the most sympathetic and active consideration.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Mr. Patrick's proposal is that Canada assume the role of a senior partner of the newly independent states, that we invite

them to join us in a monetary and customs union and that we assume responsibility for their defence and external affairs. This may appear to be a dramatic proposal, and no doubt it is, but I suggest this is one more reason for looking at it closely. It could very well be the kind of stuff which would place Canada in the world spotlight as a nation with initiative and imagination. I believe the challenge was made exactly to our size.
The West Indies have now arrived at a period of decision and this is exactly the time when Canadian assistance could make the difference between prosperity and disintegration. The proposal to which I am now referring deals only with the eight islands commonly known as "the little eight", which include Barbados, the three Leeward Islands -Antigua, St. Kitts and Montserrat-and the Windward Islands comprising Dominica, St. Lucia, St. Vincent and Grenada. The population of these eight islands is slightly above 700,000. The total land area is about half of Prince Edward Island. These islands are but three hours away from Canada by air. As a matter of fact, they are closer in terms of air distance to the capital of our country than Ottawa is to many Canadians both east and west.
The main principle behind the proposition is that these islands need our assistance and that Canada needs the West Indies. The timing of this proposition is of some importance because the Prime Ministers of these islands will be meeting with our own Prime Minister here in Ottawa next month. Moreover, Barbados will become an independent commonwealth country very shortly and Antigua will also become a self-governing state in free association with Britain. The other islands will soon achieve the same status. The year 1966 or 1967 should see the end of a century of colonial rule. These islands will be looking for a direction, a destiny, a new alliance, co-operation with other states. It is therefore the right time for Canada to become interested in dealing more intimately with these newly independent governments.
These islands need Canada because they need a new influx of capital, they are short of know-how and they will want new markets. Canada needs their climate. Canadians already provide 40 per cent of the tourist business of these islands. Under a monetary union it will be as if Canadians were spending their own money at home. This Canadian money can be used for purchases from Canada and as much needed capital for the industrial development of the islands.
June 22, 1966

The West Indies also produce now or can be placed in a position to produce goods which we are at present purchasing elsewhere. Because of the prevailing climate, which is probably the most favourable in the world for the 12 months of the year, they can produce agricultural products to be sold in Canada for an amount close to half a billion dollars a year. These figures are bound to grow with an increase in Canadian demand and an increased capability to produce on the islands. This is about the sum of money which Canadians spend every year seeking the sun in all parts of the world. The fantastic sums which Canadians now spend purchasing food outside the country and as tourists represent a drain on our balance of payments position which could partly be solved by customs and monetary union with the West Indies.
As I have said, the proposal includes our being responsible for external affairs and defence. Canada already staffs embassies throughout the world. It would seem that not much greater expense would be involved should these islands wish to be represented by our diplomats.
As to our assuming our responsibility for defence, here again arises a proposal which is worthy of consideration. We are at the present time organizing a mobile force to stand in readiness for brush-fire wars anywhere in the world. It would appear at the present time that these small wars are most likely to occur in countries with tropical or semi-tropical climates. Such being the case, why should our mobile force not train in tropical or semi-tropical climates, exactly the conditions provided by these eight little islands? Our Canadian military personnel in the West Indies would not only be in a position to get some experience in such a climate but would also provide some measure of defence to the islands. That, of course, would result in substantial economic benefit to the islands. Our armed forces personnel have already built roads, airports and other public works in many other areas of the world. Why could they not concentrate on these islands?
Our crown corporation, Air Canada, is already carrying heavy traffic during the winter to these islands. Other arrangements could be arrived at to carry not only passengers but air freight which would be of benefit both to Canada and to the West Indies.
Such a proposal for a monetary and customs union with the West Indies should be based on direct assistance and investment by
Suggested Promotion of Trade Canada for a definite period. An investment of some $20 million by way of a soft loan concentrated in one small area such as the West Indies would have a tremendous impact. It would be an investment which would bring dividends to Canadians in the near future. Canada has experts and trained personnel in various departments such as agriculture, fisheries, transport, public works, central mortgage and so on. Some of our trained people could bring fabulous assistance to the people of the West Indies. They could advise them on building homes and industries, on producing and packing the goods we cannot produce here and which we are now purchasing elsewhere.
As I stated before, the matter is of some urgency because these islands have already reached or are approaching their independence and the time for us to bring assistance and to assert our leadership is now.
Two winters ago I was in Barbados and I realized then for the first time how friendly these people were to Canadians. They probably enjoy dealing with us because we share some of their traditions and because Canadians are known as not being racially prejudiced. Many of the West Indies leaders are graduates from Canadian universities and there are more West Indies students in Canada now than in any other country.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
These islands have a long tradition of English and French culture. Barbados and Antigua have had the English culture and tradition for three centuries. St. Lucia is a bilingual country with both our official languages, French and English, and the civil code of St. Lucia is the Quebec civil code.
The Patrick proposal which I have just described has merited considerable constructive consideration in many newspaper editorials across the country, and I would like to quote from two of them. The Financial Post of June 4, 1966, had this to say:
Yet what form should this take? More aid would help. So would more soft loans. But is this enough? An imaginative program that would go much further is now being actively promoted by its author, Montreal businessman and one of the founders of Canadian Aviation Electronics, Kenneth Patrick. With the enthusiastic support of the little eight, Patrick suggests a form of Canada-West Indies integration, which would include the Canadian dollar as the standard currency throughout the islands, the removal of all customs barriers, the basing of Canadian troops in the islands for training, and the establishment of Canada as the official representative of the islands in other countries.
June 22, 1966

Suggested Promotion of Trade
It is a fresh and iconoclastic program and deserves the serious study it is now receiving in official Ottawa circles. But plainly there are troubles for everyone lurking beneath its attractive surface.
Is Patrick proposing that Canada become the new colonial power to replace Britain? If there is to be a single currency and no customs barriers, Ottawa would have to insist on maintaining considerable control of business and financial activities in the islands. This could be resented. So could the presence of Canadian troops over any long period. Would External Affairs recruit West Indians for Canada's foreign service to speak for the islands and for Canada?
These points should be discussed in official Ottawa. Canada must make clear what it requires from the islands in return for any such commitments on our part. That is the sort of talk that is needed next month. If we send the West Indians home again without having shown a real desire to talk business, we stand to pay a stiff price in later bitterness and lost opportunities.
My point, Mr. Speaker, is not that we should necessarily adopt the Patrick proposal but that it should be studied very closely by the government. It is a striking proposal, it has the merit of being new and it deserves the attention of parliament and the government.
I should like to conclude my remarks by quoting extracts from a recent editorial in the Barbados Sunday Times of June 5, 1966, entitled "Conference With A Difference":
For the second time in 40 years delegates from nearly every West Indian territory will gather to discuss relations with Canada. On the last occasion the conference was held in Ottawa without any preliminary discussion in one of these colonies. This is in modem parlance, a conference with a difference. On the last occasion the West Indies joined in establishing the Canada-West Indies trade agreement which lasted for many years and which was disrupted by the second world war. At that time all the territories were under the administrative heel of the Colonial Office. Today three of these are independent nations and the others are on the verge of independence judging by the recent offer of the British government.
As we have pointed out, many of the then dependent territories are now masters in their own house.
It is in this spirit that we enter consideration of an agenda which must bind us for good or ill to the Canadian people.

maintopic: ATLANTIC PROVINCES-NEW ENGLAND STATES AND WEST INDIES-SUGGESTED PROMOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to speak in this debate in a manner that no doubt will justify a headline, this being a case of rare unanimity within the house, because I would like to bring the support of our party to this resolution and also to commend not only the hon. member who moved it but the very constructive speech that has just been made by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Dube).

I think this resolution is extremely valuable. It has dual purposes, both of which we should approve and which certainly are very close to our hearts. Part of the resolution deals with the problem of regional development and I believe that we who come from all parts of Canada should take the question of regional development much more seriously than we do. The whole principle of regional development is one that is given a fair amount of Up service. We talk about regional development, regional balance and regional fiscal equality. These are slogans to which lip service is traditionally given in Canada, but we have failed to carry out any policy of regional equality or regional development.
I remind the house of what was stated in the 1965 annual report of the Economic Council of Canada:
Our analysis has shown that over a period of almost four decades embracing buoyant expansion, a severe depression, a prolonged war and a period of revived national growth, the regional problem in Canada has remained essentially unchanged. Large inter-regional disparities in per capita income have stubbornly persisted despite various forces working towards better balance. These have included significant redistribution of population, far reaching adjustments in the structure of economic activity at the national level, and certain public policies aimed at greater equalization of regional incomes. Against such a background, the narrowing of income disparities and the achievement of this result consistently with other basic economic and social objectives, remains one of the most difficult issues confronting the country as a whole.
It is my view that what is required is an integrated strategy of development in which the points brought forward by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) have to play their part in bringing about an adjustment of trade policies to open markets for the products of the Atlantic provinces. This, of course, is only one aspect, but it is futile for us to adopt inconsistent policies, to adopt policies of regional expenditures and incentives for regional development on the one hand and on the other hand adopt trade policies which militate against effective regional development. I think we must adopt the principle of what I call population retention.
I am happy to say that there are many people who have come to my constituency and to the Toronto urban area from the Atlantic region. I personally welcome them but I do not believe it is a healthy movement.
In the period 1941 to 1950 the Atlantic region suffered what has been described as a negative migration of 76 persons per thou-
June 22, 1966	COMMONS
sand while Ontario enjoyed a positive rate of 65 per thousand. In the period 1951 to 1960 the negative rate for the Atlantic region was 56 persons per thousand while the positive rate for Ontario was 131 per thousand. Naturally I am not objecting to the growth and development of my own province of Ontario.
I am happy to see this. But if it is caused by a forced migration, a migration forced by economic circumstances from a part of this country which has the resources and the ability to retain its population, then I say it is an unhealthy situation and all parties should accept as part of their platforms a definite policy of what I call population retention.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I do not mean by that that within the regions there is not room for manpower policies which will enable people to move from a depressed sub-region, if I may call it that, into another. I do mean that these large-scale migrations from one province to another are a totally different thing, and I think we should consider the social implications. Only too often this type of migration results in not too happy circumstances within the urban areas to which the migration comes. Sometimes, however, this is due to such things as slum conditions of which we have no reason to be proud.
This resolution deals with one aspect of the matter, that is, the trade policies which are appropriate to a policy of regional development. I believe this is extremely important to confederation as a whole. As I said, this resolution has a dual purpose. The other purpose encompassed within the resolution is the development of trade and other relations with the former British West Indies. I say nothing about New England. I should like to say, however, a word in support of what already has been said concerning our responsibilities and opportunities in Canada in respect of the West Indies.
It seems to me, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska when he referred to a press clipping from the Globe and Mail, that there are many problems to be looked into. Some form of free trade and some form of governmental assistance on a long-term basis I think are part of our international obligation. This would be beneficial not only to the islands concerned, the West Indies, but to Canada itself.
Yesterday, along with some other members of this house I visited the St. Hubert base in Quebec. As I think most hon. members who
DEBATES	6779
Suggested Promotion of Trade are familiar with matters of defence know, we are changing our defence plans and they now call less for static defences in say the European theatre of war and much more for what is referred to as a mobile force which can be moved quickly to any part of the world. Many of the areas to which such a force may have to be moved under our United Nations obligation or under some other obligation so that we can play a peacekeeping role and perhaps contribute tremendously to peace in the world are regions which are tropical or subtropical.
In Canada, with snow for a great part of the year, we cannot produce conditions of a tropical nature which our troops should have if their training is to be adequate. I am quite sure that those who are responsible for our defence policies, and particularly our mobile command, would welcome the opportunity to discuss with our friends in the West Indies the possibility of leasing training grounds. This is a prospect which should be mutually beneficial and indeed might be an addition to the security of that part of the world.
Although I know it is the usual custom of the house to talk out private members' resolutions, I do not believe there is one hon. member in this house who cannot approve of the resolution before us. It is a resolution which merely speaks of the government considering the advisability of taking the initiative in promoting increased trade. If this house were to approve of the resolution instead of throwing it out, it seems to me it would be a most encouraging instruction concerning the will of parliament on the two subject matters mainly involved, namely, regional development as it is applicable particularly to the Atlantic provinces on the one hand and international development as it affects our relations with the West Indies on the other. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I commend this resolution and I hope we will be given the opportunity to show our approval by an actual vote.

-particularly when we are considering a resolution like this one. I would very much like to see the house come to a

Suggested Promotion of Trade decision on this resolution. I know that privately all of us agree with its substance. At this moment I do not know whether this will come to pass but I hope it does. In the event that it does not, I think that today's proceedings on a matter about which there is so much agreement should suggest to us that we are impairing the reputation of this institution by continuing the process of talking out all private members' bills and ail private motions as a matter of procedure. There definitely are cases such as this one when we all agree that the motion really should be passed by the house.
For the next few minutes there are a number of things I should like to say because, along with other members, I had an opportunity this year to visit Trinidad to attend the regional conference of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. This was a great opportunity to meet with parliamentarians from this area. The impression I came away with was a very distinct one. In this area of the world the people recognize the difference between Canadians and other nationalities and they like the difference. At the same time, however, they are looking to Canada not only for increased aid and more soft loans but also for a deeper involvement on the part of Canada in their area.
I believe it is in the enlightened self-interest of our country to become more involved in this area. I read an editorial recently in the St. John's Evening Telegram which made reference to the proposal discussed by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Dube). It pointed out that six or seven years ago the government of Newfoundland subsidized a boat to travel from Newfoundland to Jamaica. This does not seem to be the kind of thing a provincial government should be doing but the sort of effort which should be expanded and promoted by the federal government in general and more particularly the other Atlantic provinces.
We do have opportunities for trade in this area. I think we must recognize that as these islands, particularly the major ones such as Trinidad and Jamaica, attempt to develop their own internal economies their traditional approach to trade may vary. We may find, as 1 believe we have, that we will lose some of our markets there because they are trying to develop their own secondary industries. I believe this presents us with the opportunity of becoming more involved with them in

their internal development so that we can assist them and at the same time help expand our own markets. So this is not something we should do because of a moral obligation we may feel for underdeveloped nations. In this particular case, as in perhaps no other, it would be very much in our self-interest and I believe this should be the basis of our approach to this area.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
In the past

this was indirectly referred to by the hon. member for Greenwood, (Mr. Brewin)-Canada has tended to look inward. Our national policy has seemed to favour the central region of Canada. I agree with him that expanding trade between the Maritimes and New England can help in regional development in Canada. I am encouraged to think that there are at least two factors at work which should help us move toward this goal. One is our sense of obligation and the other is the move generally throughout the world toward freer trade. I believe it would be very much in the interests of the four Atlantic provinces and also of Canada if we explored new avenues and took a greater interest in our approach to the problems of the West Indies, not as another country which we have to assist but as a country which has a special and unique relationship to ours and one which we can help in a special and unique way.
Before sitting down I should like to say that perhaps we might investigate the possibility of setting up a sort of Caribbean development board with representation from Canada and the countries in that area, which might in an indirect way be modelled on the Atlantic Development Board. In this way we could help these islands co-ordinate their own internal efforts for development, provide them with funds and also provide them with people who could institute these various programs. I believe this might be a step in the right direction. The suggestion of Mr. Patrick is one worthy of further study.
I am sure that all of us in this house agree that there is a great opportunity here for Canada. I hope that the coming conference to be held on July 6 will find our government taking an imaginative and understanding approach to this great challenge.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to round out the roster of speakers for the four Atlantic provinces, that area of Canada which would benefit most by increased trade with the West Indies and a new pattern of trade in

that area. It gives me pleasure to second the motion so ably proposed by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) and to speak briefly on it.
First I should like to echo the point made by some of the other speakers, that there is no reason in the world why we cannot pass this resolution before six o'clock because it is in fact a fait accompli. As the last speaker mentioned there will be a conference in Ottawa in July between the Canadian government and officials of the area known as the British West Indies which will deal with the subject matter of the resolution presented by the hon. member for Queens. We need have no qualms that governments are going to fall or be put in impossible positions if we accept the intent of this resolution. As hon. members will recall, the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) had a similar resolution on the order paper some years ago.
Recently in Halifax a three-day conference was held at Dalhousie Univeristy which was supported by the Canadian national commission for the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization and the Institute of Public Affairs of Dalhousie University. It had the blessing and, indeed, the association of the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council. It considered Canada-West Indies relations and the possibility of establishing an institute somewhere in Atlantic Canada. I understand that this possibility is still being studied. We all hope that Atlantic Canada will put its actions where its talk has been in the past. That may sound like a cynical observation, but we have received criticism in Atlantic Canada for talking too much and doing too little in the matter of better relations, trade-wise and otherwise, with the West Indies. I hope we will take the initiative in this regard and show the rest of the country that the words uttered here this afternoon have substance.
I suggest that the British West Indies delegation to the meeting to be held in Ottawa in July will make several concrete proposals, some of which have been developed by Mr. William Demas who is associated with the office of the Prime Minister of Trinidad. His suggestions deal first with tariff measures to improve trade with the West Indies. He suggested at the conference in Halifax that Canada make available more agricultural representatives to assist agricultural development in the West Indies. This, of course, would be a boon to trade between the two
Suggested Promotion of Trade countries. If they grow more they can sell more to us.
The other point I want to make relates to the warning that has been given by the education minister of Barbados, Mr. J. Cameron Tudor. He spoke at the same conference to which I referred and said that a free society will not long be retained in the West Indies if rescue operations are not set in motion immediately.
I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Halifax Mail-Star of Saturday, May 21, which reports Mr. Tudor as
follows:
He warned that the west could not expect the maintenance of the democratic tradition in the West Indies if democracy was unable to get the area out of its economic coils, and added that Canada could play a leading role in assisting the area.
I think there is a challenge here and that if we do not meet it we will be doing a grave disservice to our own country and to an aspiring democratic area which could go the other way unless we ourselves take action. It is with great pleasure, Mr. Speaker, that I second the motion presented by the hon. member for Queens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the intent of this resolution but I should like to state that the government has this matter in hand and our trade prospects under review. The government is concerned about improving trade between various parts of Canada and the rest of the world. I am concerned, however, by frequent expressions of opinion along these lines which are regional in character. These opinions have been expressed not only in the Atlantic region but also in western Canada. They relate to regional free trade arrangements involving one or two provinces and other parts of the world.
These opinions are not to be taken seriously. It would certainly undermine Canada as a nation if we were to take seriously the possibility of the establishment of special trade arrangements between other countries and particular regions or provinces in Canada. In western Canada we have heard members of provincial governments speak in this manner.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your indulgence I should like to say something about the subject matter of the debate that has taken place in the last hour. The government will take cognizance of the apparent unanimity in respect of this important subject matter. It is of importance and concern to the government and is receiving active consideration. I might say that I have a personal interest in this subject, having had a somewhat similar motion on the order paper some years ago.
I should like to indicate the business of the house for tomorrow. We propose to call legislation in the following order: First, item No. 65, second reading of the Canada Student Loans Act; item 71, second reading of the Customs Tariff bill; item 70, the Excise Tax
bill; item 49, the public utilities transfer tax resolution; item 73, the Canadian dairy commission bill; item 76, the crop insurance bill and item 48, the Canadian Livestock Feed Board resolution. If time permits we will proceed with item 62, second reading of the Canadian Film Development Corporation bill.

If the resolution concerning the small Canadian National branch lines is on the order paper tomorrow we may ask that it be considered later in the day so that the resolution can, if it is agreeable to the house, be passed and the bill circulated. Then we would have the bill available for next week.
